anomaly.name: Anomaly Watcher

extractor.core_job: Pull useful structured information from documents
extractor.name: Document Extractor

forecast.core_job: Predict what will be needed or happen next
forecast.name: Demand Forecaster

generator.core_job: Create new content from instructions or context
generator.name: Generator

recommender.core_job: Select things likely to be useful or appealing
recommender.name: Recommender

biases_limitations: Unusual behavior is not automatically harmful
Normal behavior changes over time
Rare legitimate cases can trigger alerts
Poor baselines can make anomaly scores misleading
anomaly_base.dex_entry: Quirkle represents anomaly detection: AI that learns usual patterns and flags things that look unusually different. Its tiny reptilian eyebrow rises at a strange payment, reading, or connection. A flag means "take another look," not "something bad definitely happened." Even perfectly ordinary changes can surprise a watcher that has never seen them before.
anomaly_base.input_data: Historical examples of normal behavior and new observations
anomaly_base.name: Quirkle
anomaly_base.output_data: Anomaly scores, alerts, or unusual-event flags

biases_limitations: Fraud patterns change as attackers adapt
Legitimate unusual purchases can look suspicious
Historical labels can reflect uneven scrutiny
Fraud datasets are often highly imbalanced
anomaly_fraud.dex_entry: Swindlisk represents AI fraud monitoring, which looks for unusual payments and spending patterns that may need investigation. Its suspicious snout might notice an unfamiliar location or a much larger purchase than usual. But a holiday shopping spree is not proof of crime: people must check the warning before treating an innocent customer as a fraudster.
anomaly_fraud.input_data: Transactions, account history, device information, location patterns, and customer behavior
anomaly_fraud.name: Swindlisk
anomaly_fraud.output_data: Fraud risk scores, suspicious-transaction flags, or review recommendations

biases_limitations: Failures can be too rare to model well
Different machine types have different normal behavior
Operating conditions can shift over time
Sensor failures can look like machine failures
anomaly_machine.dex_entry: Geargoyle represents AI equipment monitoring, which learns patterns in heat, vibration, and other measurements to notice possible trouble. Its stony ears perk up at the mechanical version of "that noise wasn't there yesterday." A warning can help people investigate before a breakdown, but a normal change in workload can sound suspicious too.
anomaly_machine.input_data: Vibration, temperature, pressure, equipment logs, and other machine sensor readings
anomaly_machine.name: Geargoyle
anomaly_machine.output_data: Abnormality scores, maintenance alerts, or failure-risk estimates

biases_limitations: Legitimate users can behave unpredictably
Attackers adapt to detection systems
High false-positive rates can overwhelm analysts
Monitoring can create privacy concerns
anomaly_network.dex_entry: Netnark represents AI network monitoring, which checks computer connections and activity for unusual behavior. This digital lookout may flag a burst of traffic or a login at an unexpected hour for a security team to investigate. But someone working abroad is not automatically an attacker; an unusual pattern is a clue, not a verdict.
anomaly_network.input_data: Network traffic, login behavior, connection events, and system logs
anomaly_network.name: Netnark
anomaly_network.output_data: Anomaly scores, suspicious-event alerts, or threat-priority flags

biases_limitations: Patient baselines differ
Sensors can be noisy
Too many alerts can cause alarm fatigue
Unusual measurements are not always dangerous
anomaly_vitals.dex_entry: Beatling represents AI that watches body measurements, such as heart rate, for unusual changes over time. This little rhythm keeper can flag a pattern that deserves medical attention. One odd reading may also come from exercise or a loose sensor, so its alerts need context and clinical review rather than a jump to conclusions.
anomaly_vitals.input_data: Heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood pressure, and other vital signs over time
anomaly_vitals.name: Beatling
anomaly_vitals.output_data: Anomaly scores, physiological alerts, or unusual-trend flags

biases_limitations: Performance can change with lighting
Occlusion can hide important visual information
Missing training examples can create blind spots
Models can learn visual shortcuts instead of meaningful features
False positives and false negatives are possible
detector_base.dex_entry: Seeklet represents image recognition and object detection: AI that learns from pictures to name what it sees and point out where things are. Its huge eyes can help spot a person, a product, or a damaged item. But dim lighting, hidden objects, and unfamiliar scenes can leave this eager spotter confidently confused.
detector_base.name: Seeklet
detector_base.output_data: Labels, object locations, segmentation masks, and confidence scores

biases_limitations: New packaging can differ from training data
Subtle defects can be missed
Lighting changes can reduce performance
Poor training coverage can create blind spots
detector_defect.dex_entry: Inspectra represents AI visual inspection, which checks pictures of products, food, or parts for damage and other visible problems. This fussy inspector might spot a cracked item or misplaced label before it reaches a customer. But new packaging and unfamiliar lighting can fool it into missing a flaw or treating a harmless shadow as trouble.
detector_defect.input_data: Images of products, shelves, food, or manufactured items
detector_defect.name: Inspectra
detector_defect.output_data: Product categories, defect flags, object locations, or quality assessments

biases_limitations: Performance can vary across hospitals and scanners
Underrepresented demographic groups can experience worse performance
Subtle disease patterns can be difficult to detect
Models can learn shortcuts unrelated to disease
False negatives can be especially costly
detector_disease.dex_entry: Pathogaze represents AI that checks medical images for signs of disease. It might flag a suspicious scan, point to an unusual patch, or outline tissue for a clinician to inspect. Its careful gaze is a helper, not a diagnosis: different scanners and missing examples can lead to mistakes, so medical experts must check its findings.
detector_disease.input_data: Medical images such as MRI scans, CT scans, X-rays, and pathology images
detector_disease.name: Pathogaze
detector_disease.output_data: Disease probabilities, object locations, or tissue segmentation masks

biases_limitations: Darkness can reduce detection performance
Weather can obscure visual information
Occlusion can hide people or vehicles
Distance can make small objects difficult to detect
Unusual clothing or poses can be poorly represented in training data
detector_pedestrian.dex_entry: Crowdseer represents pedestrian detection: AI that finds people in street images and video, not just whether someone is in the picture. This many-eyed lookout points out where people are so a transport system can respond. Darkness, rain, crowds, and a delivery truck hiding half the sidewalk can all make its watch less reliable.
detector_pedestrian.input_data: Camera images and video frames from streets or transportation environments
detector_pedestrian.name: Crowdseer
detector_pedestrian.output_data: Pedestrian and vehicle locations, class labels, and confidence scores

biases_limitations: Faded ink can reduce accuracy
Cursive handwriting is difficult to recognize
Damaged pages can remove information
Historical spelling and vocabulary can confuse models
extractor_archive.dex_entry: Manusqueak represents AI handwriting recognition, which turns handwritten pages into text that people can search and check. This tiny archive explorer wrestles with faded ink and elaborate old lettering instead of tidy typed words. A confident reading can still turn one name into another, so the original document and human review remain important.
extractor_archive.input_data: Scanned or photographed historical documents and handwritten records
extractor_archive.name: Manusqueak

biases_limitations: Poor scans can reduce accuracy
Handwriting can be difficult to interpret
Ambiguous language can produce incorrect extraction
Missing context can change meaning
Incorrect extracted facts can appear confident
extractor_base.dex_entry: Scribbit represents AI document extraction, which pulls useful facts such as names, dates, or amounts out of paperwork and puts them into organized fields. This tiny paper-gnawer stores the useful bits in its cheeks. Finding a word is not the same as understanding it, and a neatly filled field can still contain the wrong fact.
extractor_base.input_data: Text documents, scanned pages, forms, or document images
extractor_base.name: Scribbit
extractor_base.output_data: Structured fields, extracted entities, or machine-readable records

biases_limitations: Poor scans can create recognition errors
Handwriting quality varies
Unusual document layouts can confuse extraction
Language and accessibility differences can reduce performance
extractor_government.dex_entry: Bureaucritter represents AI form extraction, which reads scanned paperwork and places details such as names, dates, and reference numbers into usable fields. This brave little creature tackles the paperwork maze one box at a time. A smudged digit or unfamiliar form can still send a record down the wrong corridor, so important details need review.
extractor_government.input_data: Scanned forms, PDFs, document images, and handwritten fields
extractor_government.name: Bureaucritter
extractor_government.output_data: Names, dates, addresses, application fields, and other structured records

biases_limitations: Historical records are incomplete
Historical records can reflect social and institutional bias
Public documentation does not specify the exact modeling algorithm
Detected patterns still require historical interpretation
extractor_history.dex_entry: Archivole represents AI-assisted historical research, which helps people find patterns across large collections of old documents. A Friday Institute project uses AI tools to help students explore primary-source texts about redlining. This archive-burrower can surface connections that are hard to spot page by page, but incomplete records and historical prejudice still shape what it finds.
extractor_history.input_data: Large collections of primary-source historical texts
extractor_history.name: Archivole
extractor_history.output_data: Patterns, themes, or relationships for historical investigation

biases_limitations: Medical abbreviations are ambiguous
Negation can reverse the meaning of a finding
Documentation styles vary across clinicians
Health data is highly sensitive
Performance can differ across demographic groups
extractor_medical.dex_entry: Clinink represents AI medical-record extraction, which finds details such as medicines, symptoms, and dates in clinical notes. This careful note-nibbler helps organize information for people to review. "No pneumonia" and "possible pneumonia" share a tempting word but mean different things, so medical context and human checking matter far more than simple word spotting.
extractor_medical.input_data: Clinical notes, medical reports, and other healthcare text
extractor_medical.name: Clinink
extractor_medical.output_data: Diagnoses, medications, dates, procedures, and other structured clinical facts

biases_limitations: Published literature can contain publication bias
Terminology can be ambiguous across fields
Extraction can remove important context
Extracted information is not automatically true
extractor_research.dex_entry: Scholarat represents AI research extraction, which searches papers for useful facts and organizes them for comparison. This industrious reader carries findings back to the nest, helping people work through more material than they could read alone. Its strength is scale, not magical truth: missing context and weak source evidence can make an extracted fact misleading.
extractor_research.input_data: Research papers, archival text, reports, and document collections
extractor_research.name: Scholarat
extractor_research.output_data: Concepts, entities, relationships, and structured facts

biases_limitations: Handwriting can be ambiguous
Scientific names can be difficult to transcribe
Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology
Transcription errors require curator review
extractor_specimen.dex_entry: Specimunk represents AI specimen transcription, which turns handwritten collection notes into searchable electronic records. The North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and university collaborators are using AI to help transfer notes about fish specimens. This meticulous note-forager can speed up a huge task, but a misread date or place still needs a human to catch it.
extractor_specimen.name: Specimunk
extractor_specimen.output_data: Electronic specimen records and machine-readable transcriptions

signature.source_title: Museum, UNC Use AI to Transform Handwritten Records About Fish
signature.verified_use: AI-assisted transcription of handwritten fish specimen records

biases_limitations: Sudden shocks can invalidate historical patterns
Behavior can drift over time
Poor seasonality assumptions can distort forecasts
Data leakage can make evaluation unrealistically optimistic
forecast_base.dex_entry: Forespirit represents demand forecasting: AI that studies past patterns and clues such as weather or seasons to estimate what will be needed next. Its misty crystal ball might help plan stock, staffing, or transport. It is not actually psychic: a storm or an unexpected Beyoncé concert can upset its predictions.
forecast_base.input_data: Historical quantities, timestamps, seasonal patterns, and contextual variables
forecast_base.name: Forespirit
forecast_base.output_data: Future quantity estimates, forecast ranges, or predicted demand

biases_limitations: Viral events can produce unexpected demand
Cancellations can invalidate predictions
Weather can change attendance abruptly
Human behavior can shift quickly
forecast_crowd.dex_entry: Gathergeist represents AI crowd forecasting, which estimates how many people may arrive at a place or event. This sociable spirit senses a possible swarm so venues can prepare staff, food, and safety resources. Unexpected events and changing plans can still catch it out; crowds do not have to follow a tidy prediction.
forecast_crowd.input_data: Ticket sales, historical attendance, calendar information, weather, and event characteristics
forecast_crowd.name: Gathergeist

biases_limitations: Outbreaks and emergencies are difficult to predict
Historical utilization can reflect unequal access to care
Operational changes can break historical relationships
forecast_patient.dex_entry: Wardwisp represents AI patient-demand forecasting, which estimates how many people may need hospital care in the coming hours or days. This watchful spirit helps planners prepare beds, staff, and supplies before a rush. But past visits reflect who could get care as well as who needed it, so predictions can carry old gaps forward.
forecast_patient.input_data: Historical patient visits, seasonal patterns, calendar information, and local conditions
forecast_patient.name: Wardwisp
forecast_patient.output_data: Expected patient volume, bed demand, or service demand

biases_limitations: New products have little historical data
Promotions can distort historical patterns
Previous stocking decisions can influence future training data
Sudden consumer trends can invalidate forecasts
forecast_stock.dex_entry: Coinjurer represents AI inventory forecasting, which estimates how much of a product a shop may need and when. This shelf-haunting spirit tries to avoid both empty displays and piles of unwanted stock. But an empty shelf can hide real demand: yesterday's sales do not count the customers who wanted something that was already sold out.
forecast_stock.input_data: Sales history, promotions, prices, seasonal patterns, and inventory levels
forecast_stock.name: Coinjurer
forecast_stock.output_data: Future units demanded or recommended inventory quantities

biases_limitations: Construction can rapidly change travel patterns
Special events can create unusual demand
Route changes can invalidate old patterns
Long-term travel behavior can drift
forecast_transit.dex_entry: Commutoracle represents AI transit forecasting, which estimates future journeys or passenger demand from travel history, time, weather, and events. Its ghostly timetable helps planners see a possible rush coming. Then a road closes or travel habits change, and its crystal ball needs a rethink: a forecast is a guide, not a promise.
forecast_transit.input_data: Ridership, traffic, weather, calendar information, and route history
forecast_transit.name: Commutoracle
forecast_transit.output_data: Future ridership, traffic volume, or station demand

biases_limitations: Generated content can contain hallucinations
Training data can contain social and cultural bias
Provenance and copyright can be difficult to determine
Outputs can vary across repeated generations
generator_base.dex_entry: Purrrompt represents generative AI: systems that make new text, pictures, or other content from instructions and learned patterns. This eager creator can produce a story, an explanation, or a draft in moments. New does not mean true, though; an answer can sound polished and confident while getting important facts completely wrong.
generator_base.input_data: Prompts, context, reference data, or random noise
generator_base.name: Purrrompt
generator_base.output_data: Newly generated text, images, audio, or other media

biases_limitations: Generated facts can be incorrect
Official sources can be outdated
Workflow-specific details can be misunderstood
Human review remains necessary
generator_catalog.dex_entry: Catalogar represents AI-assisted catalog writing, which drafts clear, consistent descriptions of items from source information. North Carolina State University Libraries used an AI coding assistant to research and rewrite equipment and software descriptions, with staff reviewing the drafts before publication. This orderly catalog keeper can reduce repetitive writing, but polished descriptions still need factual checks.
generator_catalog.input_data: Existing device and software catalog records, official documentation, and structured instructions
generator_catalog.name: Catalogar
generator_catalog.output_data: Standardized draft descriptions and example use cases for catalog items

Training data and prompts can introduce bias
Friendly tone can be mistaken for accuracy
Human design decisions strongly shape chatbot behavior
generator_classroom_chatbot.dex_entry: Lecturlynx represents classroom chatbots: AI systems that generate conversational replies for learning activities. Friday Institute researchers worked with students to build, test, and revise such chatbots while exploring accuracy and trust. This curious classroom companion makes the machinery worth questioning, because a friendly, confident reply can still contain an invented fact.
generator_classroom_chatbot.input_data: Student-defined purpose, audience, prompts, rules, knowledge boundaries, and conversation
generator_classroom_chatbot.name: Lecturlynx

Small prompt changes can alter behavior
Retrieved information can be stale or incorrect
Fluent language can cause users to overtrust the system
generator_conversational.dex_entry: Meowlogue represents conversational AI, which generates replies to questions and instructions in an ongoing chat. This friendly talker can help draft text, explain an idea, or clarify a request. Its fluent voice is not proof of reliable knowledge: it may misunderstand, leave out context, or invent a convincing answer that needs checking.
generator_conversational.input_data: Conversation history, user requests, contextual information, and optional external tools or sources
generator_conversational.name: Meowlogue
generator_conversational.output_data: Natural-language responses, clarifying questions, or requested actions

biases_limitations: Training data can contain bias
Provenance can be unclear
Outputs can contain visual or factual artifacts
Generated work can imitate styles found in training data
Results are sensitive to prompts
generator_creative.dex_entry: Articlaw represents generative AI that makes pictures, stories, music, and other creative work from instructions or examples. This flamboyant creator turns a prompt into something new rather than simply finding an existing work. Its creations can look convincing, but a realistic image is not proof that the pictured scene ever existed.
generator_creative.input_data: Text prompts, image prompts, audio prompts, reference media, or creative constraints
generator_creative.name: Articlaw
generator_creative.output_data: Generated images, stories, music, audio, or other creative media

biases_limitations: Generated details can be incorrect
Source material can be outdated
Style can be inconsistent
Fluent output can encourage automation bias
generator_document.dex_entry: Quillcat represents AI document generation, which drafts or rewrites text from instructions and source material. This diligent writer tackles repetitive descriptions and rough first drafts so people have something to edit. Smooth sentences are not a fact check: important names, details, and claims still need someone who knows the subject to review them.
generator_document.input_data: Existing records, instructions, source documents, reference material, and formatting constraints
generator_document.name: Quillcat
generator_document.output_data: Draft documents, rewrites, summaries, or standardized descriptions

biases_limitations: Generated facts can be wrong
Content can be pedagogically weak
Material can be inappropriate for a learner's context
Overreliance can reduce human judgment
generator_learning.dex_entry: Learnx represents AI learning-content generation, which drafts explanations, questions, and activities from a teacher's instructions. This eager classroom creator can save preparation time and offer another way to explain an idea. But sounding educational is not the same as helping someone learn: teachers need to check accuracy, reading level, and whether the activity actually fits.
generator_learning.input_data: Learning goals, source material, learner context, and instructional prompts
generator_learning.name: Learnx
generator_learning.output_data: Explanations, questions, activities, examples, or instructional drafts

biases_limitations: Polished output can hide shallow reasoning
Generated pedagogy can be incorrect or inappropriate
Teacher expertise remains necessary for evaluation
Model suggestions can influence teacher decision-making
generator_lesson_planner.dex_entry: Planthera represents an AI lesson-planning assistant, which suggests teaching activities and lesson outlines from a teacher's instructions. Friday Institute researchers studied experienced teachers using Gemini to plan reading lessons and decide which suggestions to revise or reject. This classroom prowler supplies possibilities, not teaching judgment; the teacher still knows the learners and must check the plan.
generator_lesson_planner.input_data: Grade level, classroom context, student performance, instructional goals, and teacher prompts
generator_lesson_planner.name: Planthera
generator_lesson_planner.output_data: Lesson ideas, instructional drafts, activities, and lesson-plan components

In the Friday Institute's EcoJourneys science game, AI software helps provide tailored feedback for individuals and groups. This feather-changing guide tries to keep pace with learning, but its view of a student's understanding is incomplete and its advice needs checking.

Collection data can contain historical and cultural biases
Curatorial taste is subjective
The system has limited understanding of physical exhibition context
recommender_ai_curator.dex_entry: Muselect represents AI-assisted art curation: software that helps choose artworks and arrange an exhibition. At Duke's Nasher Museum of Art, ChatGPT helped select works and draft exhibition text from collection information in a curatorial experiment. This discerning bird can suggest surprising connections, but museum staff still need to check facts, context, and what the selection leaves out.
recommender_ai_curator.input_data: Machine-readable museum collection records and curatorial prompts
recommender_ai_curator.name: Muselect
recommender_ai_curator.output_data: Selected artworks, exhibition themes, interpretive text, and installation suggestions

biases_limitations: New users and items create cold-start problems
User feedback is often sparse
Popular items can dominate recommendations
Feedback loops can narrow exposure
Engagement is not the same as satisfaction
recommender_base.dex_entry: Suggestle represents recommendation systems: AI that sorts many choices to suggest things a person may find useful or appealing. This excitable bird chirps, "Try this one!" after studying clues such as earlier choices or similar interests. Helpful suggestions can reduce overload, but always offering familiar options can narrow what someone gets to discover.
recommender_base.input_data: User interactions, item information, preferences, and contextual signals
recommender_base.name: Suggestle

biases_limitations: Feedback loops can narrow exposure
Popular content can crowd out niche content
Engagement optimization can conflict with user well-being
Repeated recommendations can create filter bubbles
recommender_content.dex_entry: Reelure represents AI content recommendations, which suggest songs, films, articles, or other media based on signs of interest. Its flashy feathers tempt you toward the next discovery. Predicting another click is not the same as choosing something worthwhile, though; what keeps a person watching may not be what they actually value.
recommender_content.input_data: Viewing history, listening history, clicks, ratings, and content metadata
recommender_content.name: Reelure
recommender_content.output_data: Ranked recommendations for media, art, articles, or entertainment

biases_limitations: Performance is not the same as understanding
Learner state is only partially observable
Personalization can narrow exploration
Historical learning data can reflect unequal opportunity
recommender_learning.dex_entry: Curriquill represents AI learning recommendations, which suggest a practice problem, reading, or explanation that might help a student next. This thoughtful bird watches for clues about progress before offering another branch to explore. But a click or a wrong answer cannot reveal everything about a learner's needs, motivation, or understanding.
recommender_learning.input_data: Learner history, performance, interests, activity, and available learning resources
recommender_learning.name: Curriquill
recommender_learning.output_data: Ranked learning resources or recommended next activities

biases_limitations: Sparse history limits personalization
Preferences change with context
Popularity can dominate suggestions
Allergies and medical restrictions cannot be treated as probabilistic guesses
recommender_menu.dex_entry: Nibblet represents AI menu recommendations, which use food preferences to suggest dishes a diner may enjoy. This curious bird flits between choices asking, "What sounds good today?" Guessing taste can be helpful, but allergies and medical restrictions are not guesses to get almost right: they need firm safety rules and reliable information.
recommender_menu.input_data: Past orders, stated preferences, dietary constraints, menu items, and current context
recommender_menu.name: Nibblet

biases_limitations: Popularity can dominate recommendation lists
Sparse histories make personalization difficult
Purchases are imperfect signals of preference
Recommendations can reinforce past behavior
recommender_product.dex_entry: Cartivore represents AI product recommendations, which use shopping clues to suggest items someone might like. This collector of shiny bargains may offer a useful accessory or a similar product from a huge catalog. But one lamp purchase does not make lamps your whole personality: past behavior is an imperfect guide to what you want now.
recommender_product.input_data: Product views, purchases, ratings, user behavior, and product metadata
recommender_product.name: Cartivore

biases_limitations: Corpus coverage limits what can be recommended
Citation and popularity patterns can shape results
Semantic matching can misunderstand user intent
A recommendation is not evidence that a source is trustworthy
recommender_research.dex_entry: Referaptor represents AI research recommendations, which suggest scholarly papers related to a piece of writing. North Carolina State University Libraries offers Keenious, a tool that analyzes text to find relevant publications. This paper-carrying bird can uncover sources you did not know to seek, but a promising recommendation is not proof that a paper provides good evidence.
recommender_research.input_data: User writing, thesis statements, outlines, or research topics
recommender_research.name: Referaptor

biases_limitations: Vocabulary mismatch can hide relevant results
Embeddings can reflect training-data bias
Incomplete indexes limit what can be found
Relevance is not the same as truth
retriever_base.dex_entry: Searchound represents AI-assisted information retrieval: search systems that find existing material relevant to a request. This eager fetcher may match exact words or look for related meanings to bring back a useful document or product. A result that seems similar is not necessarily the right answer, so people still need to check what it actually says.
retriever_base.input_data: Search queries and indexed documents, products, records, or other searchable items
retriever_base.name: Searchound
retriever_base.output_data: Ranked existing items or documents judged relevant to the query

biases_limitations: Documents can be stale
Organizational knowledge can be incomplete
Poor permission controls can expose restricted information
Bad retrieval can cause downstream systems to answer from the wrong source
retriever_knowledge.dex_entry: Cognicollie represents AI-assisted knowledge search, which finds relevant passages in an organization's policies, manuals, and reports. This steady herder gathers scattered information so people can locate it more easily. An outdated or irrelevant document can still lead someone astray, especially if another system uses the result to write a confident-sounding answer.
retriever_knowledge.input_data: User questions and indexed organizational documents, policies, manuals, reports, or knowledge-base content
retriever_knowledge.name: Cognicollie

biases_limitations: Catalog metadata can be incomplete
Synonyms can be represented poorly
Ranking incentives can conflict with relevance
Sponsored results can influence ordering
retriever_product.dex_entry: Bargainbeagle represents AI product search, which finds catalog items related to a shopper's everyday description rather than needing an exact product name. This keen-nosed scout can look for "comfortable black shoes for standing all day." Matching words and meanings cannot guarantee comfort, and the order of results may reflect sales goals as well as relevance.
retriever_product.input_data: Shopper queries and indexed product catalogs
retriever_product.name: Bargainbeagle
retriever_product.output_data: Ranked products that match the shopper's request

biases_limitations: Undigitized records cannot be retrieved
Poor metadata can hide relevant documents
Incomplete collections create blind spots
Finding a document does not determine its legal meaning
retriever_records.dex_entry: Dachshundex represents AI-assisted records search, which finds existing laws, permits, and public documents relevant to a request. This long-bodied filing-cabinet explorer helps people find a useful starting point more quickly. Finding a document that mentions a problem does not explain its legal meaning or guarantee it is the current version, so careful review still matters.
retriever_records.input_data: User questions, search terms, and indexed laws, permits, or public records
retriever_records.name: Dachshundex
retriever_records.output_data: Ranked relevant public records, laws, permits, or government documents

biases_limitations: Database coverage limits what can be found
Publication and citation bias affect available literature
Queries can be interpreted incorrectly
Ranking bias can privilege already-prominent sources
retriever_research.dex_entry: Labraquery represents AI-assisted research search, which helps find scholarly papers related to a question even when they use different words. This determined literature sniffer follows ideas as well as exact phrases. A high search position is a suggestion about relevance, not a certificate of truth; researchers still need to read and judge the evidence.
retriever_research.input_data: Research questions, keywords, topics, and indexed scholarly literature
retriever_research.name: Labraquery
retriever_research.output_data: Ranked papers, books, or research sources

biases_limitations: Search is limited by database coverage
